```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
```

# Problem 1
```{r}
# Check for duplicate birthdays
birthday = function(n) { 
sim_data = sample(1:365, n, replace = TRUE)
num_bday = n_distinct(sim_data)
num_bday < n
}

# Run function 10,000 times from groups between 2 & 50
sim_results_df = expand_grid(sample_size = 2:50, iter = 1:10000) |>
mutate(duplicate = map(sample_size, birthday)) |>
unnest(duplicate)
head(sim_results_df)

#Probability that at least 2 people share a birthday
sim_results_df |>
group_by(sample_size) |>
summarize(emp_mean = mean(duplicate)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = sample_size, y = emp_mean)) + geom_point() + 
geom_line() + 
labs(
title = "Probability that at least 2 people share a birthday", 
x = "group size", 
y = "Probability of shared birthday"
)

```

Sample() was used to draw a random birthday for each person in a group. Then n_distinct() was used to check if any birthdays were repeated. We got TRUE as the answer if at least two people shared a birthday, and FALSE if not. Then expand_grid() and map() were used to run the function 10,000 times for each group size between 2 and 50. Group_by() and summarize() were then used to find the probability of finding a shared birthday by finding the average across the 10,000 runs. 

As seen in the plot, the probability of having a shared birthday increases as the group size increases. The probability is close to 0 for smaller groups and was approximately 0.98 for groups of 50 people.

# Problem 2
```{r, message = FALSE}
# Creating dataframe with all file names
full_df = tibble(
files = list.files("data/"), path = str_c("data/", files)) |>
mutate(data = map(path, read_csv)) |>
unnest(data)
head(full_df)

# Tidy data
tidy_df =
full_df |>
mutate(
files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
arm = str_sub(files, 1, 3)) |>
pivot_longer(
week_1:week_8,
names_to = "week",
values_to = "outcome",
names_prefix = "week_") |>
mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
select(arm, subject_id = files, week, outcome)

head(tidy_df)

# Make a spaghetti plot of observations on each subject over time
tidy_df |>
ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subject_id, color = arm)) + 
geom_point() + 
geom_path() + 
facet_grid(~arm) +
labs(title = "Observations on each subject over time", 
x = "Week",
y = "Outcome",
color = "Arm")

```

List.files() was used to make the data frame with all of the file names, and map() and read_csv() were used to get the data for each subject. Str_replace() and str_sub() were then used to get the subject ID and arm from the file names, and pivot_longer() was used to tidy each of the weekly observations, so each row had one subject per week. As seen in the spaghetti plot, individuals in the control arm had relatively constant outcomes between -2.5 and ~4 over the 8-week time period. In the experimental arm, individuals increased from 0 to 3 in the first week to 3 to ~7 at the end of the 8 weeks. Therefore, the experimental arm had higher outcomes on average compared to the control arm.

# Problem 3
```{r}
# Set up simulation to explore power in 1-sample t-test
sim_ttest = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
sim_data = tibble(
x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
)
sim_data |>
pull(x) |>
t.test(mu = 0) |>
broom::tidy() |>
select(estimate, p.value)
}

#Test function
sim_ttest(0)
sim_ttest(6)

# Generate 5000 datasets for mu = {1,..,6}
sim_results_df = expand_grid(
true_mu = 0:6,
iter = 1:5000) |>
mutate(estimate_df = map(true_mu, sim_ttest)) |>
unnest(estimate_df)
head(sim_results_df)

# Make a plot for the power of the test
sim_results_df |>
group_by(true_mu) |>
summarize(power = mean(p.value < 0.05)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
labs(
title = "Power of the one-sample t-test depending on mu",
x = "True value of mu",
y = "Proportion of times null was rejected (power)"
)

```

Group_by() and summarize() were used in order to find the power of each value of mu. This was done by running 5,000 tests and looking at the proportion of tests where the null was rejected. This was done when the p-value was less than the alpha value of 0.05. As seen in the plot, as the true value of mu (which is the effect size) increases, the power increases.

```{r}
# Average estimate and true value of mu
mu_df = sim_results_df |>
group_by(true_mu) |>
summarize(avg_mu = mean(estimate)) |>
mutate(samples = "Average of all samples")

# Average estimate of mu for samples with null rejected
null_rejected_df = sim_results_df |>
filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
group_by(true_mu) |>
summarize(avg_mu = mean(estimate)) |>
mutate(samples = "Average of samples with null rejected")

#Overlay plots 
bind_rows(mu_df, null_rejected_df) |>
ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_mu, color = samples)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + labs(
title = "Average estimate of mu v. true value of mu", 
x = "True value of mu",
y = "Average estimate of mu",
color = "Samples"
)
```

As seen in the plot above, the average estimate of mu in the samples where the null was rejected was fairly consistent with the average of all the samples where mu was 4 or larger. However, for values of mu that are below 4, the average of samples where the null was rejected was higher than the true value of mu, which is where we see the gap in the lines. This is because the power is low for these values of mu, and since the mu is small, the null is only rejected when a sample has a high estimate, leading to a larger average. When mu is larger, most samples rejected the null, leading to averages that are similar to each other.
